ctx.x: Well, I was working down there with Buster Bennett like I said, at the old Tuxedo Inn, and it kind of closed, and I went back out hustling again with the fellows. And we wound up one night -- we went up to Harry James -- across the street from the Hotel Sherman, the Panther Room, and he was sitting in a little bar, and he come over and said, 'Come on in -- maybe you could join the tail end of the show and see what you can do.' And they had -- I'll never forget this --

Meade Lux Albert Ammons they had Meade Lux Lewis, Alan Edwards, Joe Turner, Pete Johnson, and the Harry James band, and Frank Sinatra was singing with them. And I don't know -- I hope I don't get in no trouble for saying it, but I met him, and we come back stage and the guys were saying just stand here, they were playing; they had just broadcasted -- they were broadcasting nightly -- and Sinatra was just talking to them; he said, "I'm Frank Sinatra" and he says "You hungry?" and I said, "Yeah" and he went back…

And after he came back from singing he says, "I'm gonna be a big star one of these days. This is my last week, and I'm going with Tommy Dorsey." And I was amazed that he'd even talk to me, you know. Like I said, I was just a kid, and being on the South Side, you didn't fraternize too much with the white people, you know.

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee does not mention James Pete Johnson; the mention comes from the Interviewer referencing Duke Ellington's experience with Johnson.

ctx.x: sure enough, there was Johnny Griffin, Lou Cannon, Johnnie James on alto; Wilbur Campbell, Junior Mance, John Jenkins we got in the studio, and I just said what we gonna play -- and we run it down, and we did it. Well, that's something -- most of the things were like that, and I think Johnson had one tune that he, that he said he arranged, you know.

But that's not to be taken lightly, because I was thinking about what Duke said about having to learn music two different ways, and he was taught how to learn music, but then he heard James Pete Johnson, and that was a different experience; a different learning experience, and he ended up memorizing things in a way that is very unusual, very peculiar. So I think that's important that you just went in and recorded that, and the end result is Chicago sound, because that's a very beautiful notable album.
Well, yes. I'm of the school where we could play; we look at each other and we'd have an arrangement; I mean, you just have this feeling for one another.
